headline: The Government legislates where the phone makers would not, and the Health Bill leaves the Commons

departments.department: Department of Health and Social Care
Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs
Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade

intro: In June the Government gave the technology companies three months to make it impossible for a child to take or share a nude image on a phone. On Tuesday afternoon the three months were up. Lisa Nandy told the House that Apple and Google had made “meaningful changes at operating level” and that “the truth is that they do not meet the scale of this crisis”, and that her officials had that day begun drawing up a Bill to compel what the deadline had not. She put the case in numbers taken from the Internet Watch Foundation and her own Department: 91 per cent of the images are self-generated by children, around 9,000 child sexual abuse offences a year involve an online element, and under-18s are the subject of almost a quarter of online blackmail. Around it the House gave the Health Bill its remaining stages over two long evenings, dividing six times and winning six times, three of them with Labour alone in the No lobby; a Minister explained a weekend of masked protest at Dover and at Portsmouth harbour; and 1,814 written questions were tabled by 223 Members, one of whom asked the same Department six different questions about the same policy and received the same answer six times.
body: Lisa Nandy rose at 3.31 pm on Tuesday to report on a deadline of the Government’s own setting. In June the technology industry had been challenged “on a three-month timeline” to produce road maps for device-level protections that would stop children taking, sharing or viewing nude images on phones and tablets; since then, officials from her Department and the Home Office had run what she called “an unprecedented work programme with Apple and Google.” The report was not a failure and not a success. Both companies “have provided the Government with significant commitments”; there had been “progress in the blocking, not blurring, of nude imagery on underage devices,” building on Apple’s roll-out this year of operating-system-level age assurance. “These proposals are a step in the right direction,” the Secretary of State said. “However, the truth is that they do not meet the scale of this crisis.” She gave the scale in figures. The Internet Watch Foundation believes 91 per cent of these images are self-generated by children; around 9,000 child sexual abuse offences each year involve an online element; under-18s are the subject of almost a quarter of online blackmail. So the Government will legislate, with primary legislation to require the major platforms to build device-level protections in, and a second requirement that apps used by children prevent them accessing or sharing nudity. The escape clause was left open and then closed by hand. If platforms build the thing themselves, “we will of course reassess whether legislation is necessary,” but “based on what I have seen in progress over the last three months, it is almost certain that we will be legislating in this area.” Her officials, she said, had begun work that day. “We will give tech companies the chance to lead; we will not give them the chance to lag.” The claim she attached to it, that the measures “will make Britain the first country in the world to go this far”, is the Government’s, made twice at the Dispatch Box and endorsed from the Benches behind her by Liz Kendall as “a world first”; this paper records it as a claim and not as a fact.

The House did not divide on any of it, and the objections were about clocks rather than principles. Rebecca Paul, the shadow Secretary of State, opened by remembering “16-year-old Murray Dowey, who took his own life just hours after being tricked into sending an intimate image online,” welcomed the device-level commitment as “a huge practical step,” and then put the sharp question: “‘as soon as we can’ is not yet a timetable.” Anna Sabine, for the Liberal Democrats, was blunter, saying “this announcement could have been made three months ago”, and asked for an assurance that the Bill would proceed whatever the companies did. It would, Ms Nandy said. Jess Phillips, who has resigned from government twice, observed that “this statement and the previous one are about the two things that I have previously resigned over, so I feel that my moral compass is back,” and then made the argument that decides the privacy question: “there is no privacy issue if we just stop children taking images in the first place”, and “the image will not exist to be able to go anywhere.” On the adjacent measure the record is firmer than the statement. Asked by Bell Ribeiro-Addy whether the Online Safety Act’s powers would enforce the coming minimum age, the Department answered on Monday that regulations for the under-16 social media ban are to be laid “by the end of this year, with the restrictions in effect from Spring 2027”; a second answer, on Tuesday, confirmed the model would follow Australia’s, catching “services such as Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and X.” Ms Kendall, thanking the Secretary of State from the Government Benches, described the same ban as coming into effect “early next year.”

The legislative work of the week was the Health Bill, which took two evenings to finish and produced six divisions, all six lost by the Opposition and three of them decided by the governing party voting on its own. On Monday night Helen Morgan’s new clause 6, every maternity unit rated “good” or “outstanding”, a Director of Midwifery in every maternity service, ringfenced development funding, a dedicated neonatal workforce plan, fell at 10 pm by 77 to 317, with 317 Labour Members and nobody else in the No lobby. Fourteen minutes later came the gravest vote of the week. Dr Caroline Johnson’s new clause 145 asked for one sentence of statute, requiring that the Secretary of State “must, within 30 days of the day on which this Act is passed, publish the Government’s response to the Hughes Report” on redress for those harmed by valproate and pelvic mesh. It fell by 170 to 316, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Democratic Unionists, Plaid Cymru, the Greens, Reform UK and the independents together, against Labour alone. On Wednesday 2 September, the first day of this window, Dr Johnson had also asked the Department in writing when it intends to respond to the Hughes Report at all. The reply came on Tuesday, the day after the House refused her deadline: “The Department of Health and Social Care has indicated that it will not be possible to answer this question within the usual time period.” Tuesday evening produced four more divisions in thirty-eight minutes, on corridor care, to be ended within a year or made the subject of an independent inquiry, 79 to 300; a ban on prescribing puberty blockers to under-18s for gender dysphoria, 108 to 357, with three Labour Members (Graham Stringer, Mary Glindon and Jonathan Hinder) in the Aye lobby and the Liberal Democrats against it but for Angus MacDonald, who was not; single-sex staff facilities, 106 to 302; and, at 6.39 pm, Dr Johnson’s amendment 1, to strike out the clause transferring the Health Services Safety Investigations Body’s functions to the Care Quality Commission, which drew the largest Opposition vote of the week at 162 to 297. Twelve minutes later Yvette Cooper moved the Third Reading, and no division was called on it. Damian Hinds, opposite her, did the arithmetic of the Bill’s own passage: “she is the third Secretary of State for this Bill. It was about 40 minutes after First Reading that the right hon. Member for Ilford North (Wes Streeting) resigned. I wonder which bit he had just spotted.”

The rest of the week arrived as statements and urgent questions, and the largest of them was the Foreign Secretary's on Tuesday, which moved the British Government from calling the settlements illegal to calling the occupation itself unlawful and announced an import ban on settlement goods, a new sanctions regime aimed at settlements rather than at Israel, and an arms export ban that now lasts as long as the occupation does. On Monday evening Sarah Jones, the Minister for Policing and Crime, set out the facts of the weekend on the south coast. At about half past seven on Saturday morning around 150 people, many in face coverings, descended on the port of Dover in what Kent police called a “no-notice” protest, and no arrests were made; on Sunday afternoon a boat carrying approximately 120 people reached British waters near the Isle of Wight and was directed into Eastney marina, where by 8 pm more than 200 protesters, “many of those protesters dressed in all black and wearing face masks,” had gathered to block three coaches. Officers used a dispersal notice, batons and PAVA spray, and worked until about four in the morning. Chris Philp said 625 people had crossed the Channel the previous day; the Minister answered with 48,000 attempted crossings prevented in partnership with French law enforcement, a 43 per cent fall in crossings on last year, and £110 million of the French money now contingent on results. On Thursday Angela Rayner took the high street and the pavement together, closure orders doubled from six to twelve months, £6 billion for Pride in Place, and £442 million for a rough sleeping programme under which “by Christmas this year, everyone sleeping rough will be offered a route off the streets,” eight in ten of them, she noted, with a mental health vulnerability. Two urgent questions were granted the same day: Robbie Moore on bluetongue, where 795 cases have been confirmed in Great Britain since the first serotype 3 case in Staffordshire on 10 July, and Andrew Bowie, three days into the shadow energy brief, on Jackdaw and Rosebank, where the answer was that both fields remain “subject to a live regulatory process” and decisions will come “in due course”, an answer repeated to the Lords on Monday. The window opened on 2 September with the Representation of the People Bill’s Report stage and its Third Reading by 411 to 102, and it reached the Lords the next day. Alex Sobel asked leave on Tuesday to bring in a Bill prohibiting artificial superintelligence, quoting Professor Stuart Russell on governments permitting private entities “to essentially play Russian roulette with every human being on earth”; Sir Bernard Jenkin, opening with “I am as keen as anybody to get on with discussing the Health Bill,” commended the speech, opposed the Bill so that the argument might continue, and lost. Leave was given, and the Second Reading is set for 13 November. The oddest division of the week was on Friday morning, when Ruth Jones moved that the House sit in private and was the only Member to vote for it: 1 to 79, most of the Noes her own colleagues. The same statement sanctioned Hezbollah's financing arm, reported Iran to the United Nations Security Council and reimposed major economic sanctions on it, and set aside a further 250 million pounds against antisemitism at home. Tom Tugendhat answered for the Opposition by starting with what both sides agree on; Emily Thornberry, whose Committee had asked for this unanimously more than a year ago, said only At last; Jeremy Corbyn pressed for more, naming the surveillance flights over Gaza and the Elbit Systems factories in this country. The legislation is to be in place within six to nine months.

Beneath the Chamber the register returned to its ordinary volume: 1,814 questions tabled by 223 Members over five days, against the 6,683 of the week before. The Conservatives tabled 721, Labour 452 and the Liberal Democrats 307; Health took 242, Housing 209 and the Home Office 156. Mike Wood put 95, sixty-one of them to the Cabinet Office and still circling No 10 North; David Reed put ten on the composition of the official reserves and the country’s exposure to dollar-denominated assets; Dr Al Pinkerton put seven on the cost of managing reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete at Frimley Park Hospital until its replacement opens. The wry note belongs to the Ministry of Justice, which on Tuesday answered twenty-two of Ben Obese-Jecty’s questions from last week’s 703 with the identical sentence, prison by prison from Holloway to Ashwell: “The Ministry of Justice does not hold total figures for investment in improving the physical condition of prisons between 1997 and 2010.” The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport managed a purer form of the genre, telling Mr Wood that it could not say what had been budgeted for digital identity cards because “a full business case had not yet been finalised prior to the cancellation of the national Digital ID programme.” The grave note belongs to Shivani Raja, whose cluster on domestic abuse and suicide was answered across three departments in the same week that Liz Twist secured a Westminster Hall debate for World Suicide Prevention Day, which falls on Thursday. The Home Office confirmed that it funds the Domestic Homicide Project, which recorded 150 suspected domestic-abuse-related suicides, and that it funds Advocacy After Fatal Domestic Abuse for families bereaved by them; the Department of Health and Social Care, asked about research suggesting domestic abuse may contribute to up to 1,000 suicides a year, replied that the Secretary of State “will address these and related issues further in the coming months.” The Department for Education, asked about the independent review of deaths among care-experienced young adults published on 25 August, called “the shockingly high number of early deaths of care experienced young people” a national tragedy, said it is working at pace, and confirmed that the Staying Close duty becomes national in 2029. The register holds 649. Holborn and St Pancras has had no Member for eight days and no writ has moved.

feature.title: Six questions, one answer, six times
feature.department: Department of Health and Social Care
feature.status: written questions tabled 2–8 Sep; 26 to Health, 11 to the Foreign Office, none to Energy Security and Net Zero
feature.summary: Dr Luke Evans shadowed health for twenty-one months. On 31 August he was moved to Energy Security and Net Zero. In the first sitting week of his new brief he tabled fifty-eight written questions, twenty-six of them to the Department he had just left and not one to the Department he had just joined; the nearest he came to his own portfolio was asking the Foreign Office what criteria it would use before consenting to a new petroleum exploration licence. The reshuffle of 31 August that moved him also made Andrew Bowie shadow Energy Secretary, and on 3 September Mr Bowie was at the Dispatch Box with an urgent question on Jackdaw and Rosebank while his new junior spent the day tabling questions about mental health estates. The health questions are not a valedictory sweep but an audit, and they arrive in two files. The first, eleven questions tabled on 3 September, takes apart the £343 million announced on 5 August for community mental health centres and mental health emergency departments and asks the questions an announcement does not answer, among them what proportion is capital, what estate the fifty-nine emergency departments will occupy and how many need new buildings, what criteria fixed their locations, which professional groups will staff the 159 new facilities, whether the workforce for them is new recruitment or redeployment, and whether that estimate has reached the NHS workforce plan at all. The second file is the one that repays reading. Over 2 and 3 September he put six separate questions on Advice and Guidance, the pathway by which a general practitioner seeks specialist advice instead of making a referral, each citing a different published finding, one being the Royal College of Physicians’ survey that 89 per cent of the physicians delivering it have had no formal training and that 47 per cent have no dedicated time for it in their job plans; Pulse’s survey that general practitioners estimate 36 per cent of unsolicited Advice and Guidance responses ask for work outside the remit of general practice, and that around a quarter of referrals come back as unsolicited requests; and the Health Services Safety Investigations Body’s findings that poorly implemented Advice and Guidance pathways “have contributed to delayed diagnoses, missed diagnoses and delays to treatment,” together with its recommendation that NHS England and the Department undertake a rapid evaluation. On Tuesday 8 September Karin Smyth answered all six. The six answers are word for word identical. They describe the model’s merits, note 2,000 extra general practitioners since July 2024 and that 77 per cent of patients report a good overall experience with their surgery, and say an external evaluation has already been commissioned. They do not mention the Royal College of Physicians, or Pulse, or the Health Services Safety Investigations Body, and they do not say whether the recommendation is accepted. The Minister signing them spent that same evening carrying the Health Bill through its remaining stages, in the course of which the House voted by 162 to 297 to keep the clause abolishing the very body whose findings the six questions cited.
questions: Dr Luke Evans (Conservative, Hinckley and Bosworth), 58 questions over four tabling days, in the first sitting week after he moved from the health brief to energy: 26 to the Department of Health and Social Care, 11 to the Foreign Office, none to Energy Security and Net Zero.

Six questions on Advice and Guidance, each citing a different finding by the Royal College of Physicians, Pulse or the Health Services Safety Investigations Body, drew six identical answers from Karin Smyth on 8 September, none of which names any of the three.

Eleven questions take apart the £343 million announced on 5 August for 59 mental health emergency departments and 159 community facilities, capital share, estate, staffing, siting, and whether the workforce estimate has reached the NHS workforce plan.

qa.heading: Internet: Age Assurance
qa.department: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
qa.question: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, whether she is planning to use powers under the Online Safety Act to enforce planned minimum age requirements.
qa.answer: Following the Government’s recent consultation, Growing up in the online world, it was announced in June 2026 that government are banning social media companies from offering their services to under-16s. We are aiming for regulations on the social media ban to be laid before Parliament under the powers of the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 by the end of this year, with the restrictions in effect from Spring 2027.

qa.heading: Domestic Abuse: Suicide
qa.question: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, what steps her Department is taking in response to the Domestic Homicide Project’s finding of 150 suspected domestic abuse-related suicides in England and Wales; and whether the government plans to update police guidance on investigating sudden deaths where there is a history of domestic abuse.
qa.answer: This Government is committed to tackling the most severe and heartbreaking outcomes of violence and abuse, including suicides and sudden or unexplained deaths that occur following domestic abuse. It is vital that police officers understand the link between domestic abuse and suicide, and we are already taking steps to improve the police response. The Home Office funds the Domestic Homicide Project to capture information on these deaths from police forces in England and Wales and identify how the response can be improved. The Project and the College of Policing published new national policing guidance last year, highlighting the importance of considering any history of domestic abuse and applying professional curiosity at the scene of these deaths. The Home Office continues to work with the police to monitor the implementation of this guidance and has commissioned deep dives with select police forces to examine how the police are responding to suicides and unexplained deaths that follow domestic abuse following its introduction. Additionally, the Home Office recognises the devastating impact of these deaths on families. That is why we fund the organisation Advocacy After Fatal Domestic Abuse to support families bereaved by suicide following domestic abuse.

qa.heading: HMP/YOI Holloway
qa.question: To ask the Secretary of State for Justice, between 1997 and 2010, what investment did his department make in improving the physical condition of the prison estate at HMP Holloway.
qa.answer: The Ministry of Justice does not hold total figures for investment in improving the physical condition of prisons between 1997 and 2010. During that period, expenditure on the prison estate took a number of forms, including centrally managed maintenance and development programmes, locally-funded maintenance activity, and capital investment. These categories of expenditure were recorded using multiple systems, and the methods of recording changed over time. As a result, the Department is unable to provide a consistent and reliable figure for investment in the physical condition of individual prison establishments during the specified period.

row.title: Health Bill: Report Stage: New Clause 145

votes.blurb: The gravest vote of the week, at 10.14 pm on Monday. Dr Caroline Johnson’s clause asked for one sentence of statute, that the Government publish its response to the Hughes Report on redress for those harmed by valproate and pelvic mesh within 30 days of Royal Assent. Every party in the House except one voted for it; Labour voted it down alone. Five days earlier she had asked the same Department in writing when it intends to respond at all, and was told on Tuesday that an answer was not possible “within the usual time period.”

The largest Opposition turnout of the week, at 6.39 pm. Dr Johnson again, this time to strike out clause 63 and stop the Health Services Safety Investigations Body’s functions passing to the Care Quality Commission. Conservatives, Liberal Democrats, Democratic Unionists, Reform UK, the Greens and six independents in one lobby, Labour in the other.

row.title: Health Bill: Report Stage: New Clause 142

votes.blurb: The only division of the week that split a party rather than dividing the House along it. The clause would have barred puberty blockers for under-18s treated for gender dysphoria and required a resolution of both Houses before any clinical trial. Three Labour Members (Graham Stringer, Mary Glindon and Jonathan Hinder) voted for it; the Liberal Democrats went into the No lobby but for Angus MacDonald, who went into the Aye. Defeated 108 to 357, the largest No vote of the week.

row.title: Health Bill: Report Stage: New Clause 143

votes.blurb: Single-sex changing rooms, lavatories and washing facilities for NHS staff, put on the face of the Bill. Defeated 106 to 302 at 6.28 pm, the Conservatives, Democratic Unionists, Reform UK and six independents for, Labour and the Greens against.

row.title: Health Bill: Report Stage: New Clause 140

votes.blurb: Corridor care to be ended within a year of Royal Assent, or an independent inquiry into the Department’s handling of it. Defeated 79 to 300 at 6.01 pm, a Liberal Democrat clause, carried into the lobby by the Democratic Unionists, the Greens, Reform UK and seven independents, opposed by Labour and by nobody else.

row.title: Health Bill: Report Stage: New Clause 6

votes.blurb: Helen Morgan’s maternity safety clause required every unit to be rated “good” or “outstanding” by the Care Quality Commission, a Director of Midwifery in every maternity service, ringfenced development funding and a dedicated neonatal workforce plan, with an annual report to both Houses. Defeated 77 to 317 at 10 pm on Monday, with 317 Labour Members alone in the No lobby and no Conservative in either.

row.title: Representation of the People Bill: Third Reading

votes.blurb: The window opens where the last one closed. The Bill through the Commons at 7.59 pm on Wednesday 2 September by 411 to 102, Labour, the Liberal Democrats, the Scottish National Party, the Greens and Plaid Cymru for, the Conservatives and Reform UK against. It had its First Reading in the Lords the following afternoon.

row.title: Representation of the People Bill: Report Stage: New Clause 65

votes.blurb: An independent review of how overseas electors register and vote, defeated 166 to 346 with the Liberal Democrats in the Aye lobby beside the Conservatives, the closest margin of the four that finished the Bill.

row.title: Representation of the People Bill: Report Stage: New Clause 67

votes.blurb: The Conservative clause to make it an offence to publish campaign material in a foreign language, defeated 105 to 410 with the Liberal Democrats voting against it.

row.title: Representation of the People Bill: Report Stage: New Clause 88

votes.blurb: The Liberal Democrat clause for a Royal Commission on a cap on political donations, defeated 85 to 427 with the Conservatives against, the largest No vote recorded in this window.

The oddest division of the week and the smallest Aye vote the House can produce. At 9.34 on Friday morning Ruth Jones moved that the House sit in private and was the only Member to vote for it. Seventy-nine voted against, most of them her own Labour colleagues, and both sets of tellers were Labour too. The device spent, the Child-like Sexual Abuse Dolls (Offences) Bill got its Second Reading; three other private Members’ bills were objected to and put off to another Friday.

bills.blurb: The week’s legislative centre. Report stage on Monday 7 and Tuesday 8 September, roughly eighty thousand words of debate and six divisions, all won by the Government and three of them with Labour alone in the No lobby. Yvette Cooper moved the Third Reading at 6.51 pm on Tuesday and no division was called on it. Damian Hinds noted from the Opposition front bench that she is the Bill’s third Secretary of State, the first having resigned “about 40 minutes after First Reading.” It goes to the Lords.

Through the Commons on 2 September by 411 to 102 after three Opposition new clauses fell in under an hour, and read a first time in the Lords on 3 September. The Government’s own new clauses would ban political donations in cryptoassets, retrospective to 25 March 2026.
Two committee days in the window, on 2 and 8 September, and out of committee by the end of it. The Bill is now at Report in the Lords.

row.title: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill

bills.blurb: Committee stage in Grand Committee on 3 and 7 September, and to Report thereafter, the network security Bill moving quietly in the week the Lords also asked about data security for United Kingdom citizens.
Great British Railways in Grand Committee on 8 September, while four separate written questions in the Commons asked after the same body.

overview.headline: The Government legislates where the phone makers would not, and the Health Bill leaves the Commons
overview.intro: In June the Government gave the technology companies three months to make it impossible for a child to take or share a nude image on a phone. On Tuesday 8 September the three months were up. Lisa Nandy, the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, told the House of Commons that Apple and Google had made meaningful changes at operating level, and that those changes do not meet the scale of the crisis. She put the case in figures. The Internet Watch Foundation believes 91% of these images are made by children themselves. Around 9,000 child sexual abuse offences each year involve an online element. So the Government will legislate. It will require the large platforms to build protection into the devices, and it will require apps used by children to stop them accessing or sharing nudity. Her officials began drafting that day and she gave no date. She said the measures would make Britain the first country in the world to go this far, which is the Government’s claim rather than an established fact. The rest of the week went to the Health Bill, which finished in the Commons after six votes, and to a statement on a weekend of masked protest on the south coast.

brief.title: The occupation declared unlawful, and a settlements sanctions regime
brief.note: Ed Miliband made a statement on Israel and Palestine that moved the British position. Britain has long called the settlements illegal while staying silent on the occupation as a whole, which the International Court of Justice held unlawful in 2024. The Government's official view is now that the occupation is unlawful too. He announced an import ban on goods from illegal settlements, a new sanctions regime aimed at settlements and their expansion rather than at Israel, a ban on advertising settlements here, and an arms export ban lasting as long as the occupation does. Settlers in the occupied territories have gone from about 270,000 in 1993 to some 770,000.

brief.title: Protecting children online
brief.note: Lisa Nandy told the House of Commons that a three month deadline set for the technology companies in June had not been met, and that she had instructed officials that day to begin drawing up a Bill. Rebecca Paul, the shadow Secretary of State, welcomed it and remembered 16 year old Murray Dowey, who took his own life hours after being tricked into sending an intimate image, then pressed for a date the Secretary of State would not give.

brief.title: The Health Bill finishes in the Commons
brief.note: Six divisions over two evenings, all won by the Government, and in three of them Labour was alone in the No lobby. The gravest was on Monday night, when a clause requiring the Government to publish its response to the Hughes Report on redress for those harmed by valproate and pelvic mesh within 30 days fell by 170 to 316, and Yvette Cooper moved the Third Reading at 6.51 pm on Tuesday without a division.

brief.title: Protests at Dover and Portsmouth
brief.note: Sarah Jones, the Minister for Policing and Crime, said around 150 people, many in face coverings, arrived without notice at the port of Dover on Saturday morning, and that on Sunday evening more than 200 protesters gathered at a Portsmouth marina to block three coaches carrying people from a boat of about 120. Officers used a dispersal notice, batons and PAVA spray, and worked until about four in the morning. No arrests were made on either night and investigations continue.

brief.title: Rough sleeping, bluetongue and the North Sea
brief.note: Angela Rayner told the House that £442 million has been set aside so that everyone sleeping rough is offered a route off the streets by Christmas, and that closure orders on problem shops will double from six months to twelve. Two urgent questions followed, one on bluetongue, where 795 cases have now been confirmed in Great Britain, and one from Andrew Bowie on the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil fields, which was answered again in the House of Lords on Monday.

brief.title: Value added tax comes off electricity bills
brief.note: At Prime Minister's Questions, Andy Burnham told the House: I will remove VAT from electricity bills next month. He added that it would not solve everything but would take a little pressure off, told the questioner to look out for further measures through the year, and announced a two pound cap on bus fares across England for the whole of 2027, noting that the fares cap does not apply in Scotland. He put both under one description, that this is a cost of living Government. Westminster Hall spent the day on public confidence in the police.
